knowledge.title: AI-operator self-correction: minimal surgical edits, one change per cycle, revert before the next attempt — the antidote to overthinking
knowledge.solutionUnderTest:
1) Make the smallest edit that plausibly addresses the CAUSE (anchored edit, not file rewrite). 2) ONE change per cycle; re-run the exact failing check after each change — that result is the only progress signal. 3) SELECTIVE, SAFE ROLLBACK — never blanket restores: BEFORE the first edit, capture the pre-edit content of ONLY the file(s) you are about to touch (bridge read_file, or git diff to enumerate hunks). On a failed attempt, restore exactly what you changed: git restore -p (choose your hunks), a path-limited stash (git stash push -- <paths>), or re-apply the captured pre-edit content. NEVER run repo-wide git checkout . / git reset --hard — they destroy the user's unrelated uncommitted work. If the file had PRE-EXISTING uncommitted changes, prefer restoring just your hunks over any file-level restore. CONFIRM the rollback: re-run the exact failing check — the ORIGINAL error must reproduce; that is your known-green marker. 4) CONTINUATION CRITERIA — there is no fixed attempt count. Continue surgical attempts while: (a) each attempt tests a NEW hypothesis informed by the actual error text of the previous failure; (b) the diff stays anchored at the failure site; (c) the error is changing or moving (progress signal). STOP and surface the situation to the user when: attempts repeat the same hypothesis with no new information; the diff keeps growing past the causal site; or you can no longer attribute which change did what. 5) Re-read the file after editing to confirm the edit landed as intended. 6) Re-read the ACTUAL error text (not the assumed one) before each next attempt; reduce to a minimal reproduction when the system resists. 7) Reserve full-file rewrites for files whose STRUCTURE is itself the demonstrated cause — not merely because surgical attempts failed: require structural evidence or exhausted-information signals from step 4, and surface the rewrite decision to the user whenever the blast radius is non-trivial.

VERIFICATION PLAN (PLANNED — NOT EXECUTED; no evidence exists for v2 claims yet): V1 experimental (git; scratch repo in a temp dir via mktemp -d so nothing is written into the user's workspace): seed a repo with pre-existing uncommitted changes; apply an agent-style edit; exercise the selective rollback (git restore -p / git stash push -- <path>) and verify the user's pre-existing changes SURVIVE while the agent's edit is gone; negative control: show that repo-wide git checkout . destroys them — the reason it is banned. V2 doc-based (NOT yet inspected): git restore -p and path-limited stash semantics. V3 practice-based: the continuation criteria are process guidance, not mechanically testable claims.

originalProblem.description: EXP-000012 (latest version v2, the technical revision) claims: (1) rollback must be SELECTIVE and SAFE — restore exactly what the agent changed (git restore -- <path>, git stash push -- <paths>, or re-apply captured pre-edit content), never repo-wide git checkout . / git reset --hard which destroy the user's unrelated uncommitted work; (2) when the agent's edit and the user's pre-existing WIP share ONE file, prefer restoring just the agent's hunks — the content-capture path (capture before the first edit, re-apply on failure) is the non-interactive mechanism; (3) the rollback must be CONFIRMED by re-running the exact failing check — the ORIGINAL error must reproduce as the known-green marker; (4) git restore -p and path-limited stash semantics are doc-verifiable. The v2 revision REMOVED the arbitrary two-attempt rewrite threshold (continuation is governed by information gain — process guidance, plan item V3, not mechanically testable per the record itself).

V1b: `git stash push -- lib.js` achieves the same with the change recoverable in the stash. V1c (negative control): the banned `git checkout -- .` destroys the user's WIP along with the agent's edit. V1d: when user WIP and the agent edit share one file, capturing the pre-edit content BEFORE the edit and re-applying it on failure restores the user's hunk and removes the agent's hunk, leaving the working tree at exactly the user's WIP. V2: the locally installed git documentation (man git-restore / man git-stash for git 2.53.0) documents path-scoped working-tree restore, interactive hunk selection, and stash push with pathspec.

hypothesisHistory.hypothesis: The V2 failure was a case-definition flaw, not a documentation mismatch: the man page hard-wraps the sentence 'Restore specified paths in the working tree with some contents from a restore source' across two lines, so the literal single-line grep missed it (the probe had verified the phrase exists, split by the wrap). Normalizing newlines/whitespace before matching makes all six assertions pass without weakening any of them.
hypothesisHistory.expectedObservation: V2-DOC-VERIFIED with all six phrases FOUND
hypothesisHistory.changeNote: root cause: man-page line wrapping broke a literal substring match (attempt VTA-000039 preserved: 5/6 phrases found, the wrapped one missed). Fix: the case command now pipes the man output through tr '\n' ' ' + squeeze before matching; the sandbox script was restaged with the identical normalization. No assertion was weakened.

V1b `git stash push -- lib.js` achieved the same guarantees with the stashed change recoverable in the stash list. V1c (negative control) the banned repo-wide `git checkout -- .` destroyed the user's uncommitted WIP along with the agent's edit — the demonstrated blast radius justifying the record's ban. V1d when the user's WIP and the agent's edit shared ONE file, the record's prescribed content-capture path (capture pre-edit content before the first edit, re-apply on failure) restored the user's hunk, removed the agent's hunk, and left the working tree at exactly the user's WIP (git diff non-empty, no agent content). V2 the locally installed git 2.53.0's own documentation (man git-restore, man git-stash) documents 'Restore working tree files', 'Restore specified paths in the working tree with some contents from a restore source', 'Interactively select hunks' (patch mode), 'new stash entry', 'pathspec', and the stash-push pathspec synopsis — the selective-rollback semantics are exactly as the record describes.
analyses.comparison: Every prediction matched: both selective mechanisms preserved user work while reverting exactly the agent's edit and reproducing the original error; the blanket restore destroyed user work; the mixed-file content-capture path left the tree at exactly the user's WIP; and all six documented phrases were found in the installed git's man pages after whitespace normalization.
analyses.alternativeExplanations: (1) The experiments use crafted scratch repos in mktemp dirs — they verify git's MECHANICS, not any real repository of the user; the user's actual workspace was never touched. (2) git restore -p (interactive hunk selection) could not be exercised non-interactively; its semantics are doc-verified (V2: 'Interactively select hunks') and the non-interactive content-capture path (V1d) covers the same mixed-file requirement. (3) The VM dry-run environment runs git 2.47.3 while the user machine has 2.53.0 — all four experimental behaviors were identical on both, and the doc assertions target the user machine's own man pages. (4) V3 (continuation/stop criteria) is process guidance — the record's own plan classifies it as not mechanically testable; no case was created for it.
analyses.recommendedModifications: The verified evidence supports the record's revised claims in full. For the owner's review: the two-attempt threshold removal is justified (V3 is guidance, not a rule); the selective-rollback safety property is now demonstrated for all three prescribed mechanisms (path restore, path stash, content capture) with the negative control showing why blanket restores are banned.

proposedConclusion.summary: All 5 critical test cases passed on real executions on the user's machine: path-limited restore and path-limited stash both preserve the user's uncommitted work while reverting exactly the agent's failed edit (original error reproducing as the known-green marker); the banned repo-wide checkout demonstrably destroys user work; the content-capture path handles the mixed-file case leaving the tree at exactly the user's WIP; and the installed git's own documentation states the selective semantics. The removed two-attempt threshold required no evidence (a removal, like EXP-000011's retracted superlative).
